Instagram blocked your account. Can you go to the High Court? The Delhi High Court says no, not by writ. If Meta itself blocks you, the remedy is the Grievance Appellate Committee or a civil suit. Here's the full map of where to go, from four High Court rulings in six weeks. Sarthak Bhagat v. UoI Article 226 Remedies map Adv. Ashwani Kumar · Advocate | Data Privacy & Technology Law 01 / 08

DELHI HIGH COURT · JUSTICE AMIT MAHAJAN · Sarthak Bhagat v. Union of India THE FACTS Accounts disabled without notice or reasons Instagram cited its community standards. The in-app review failed. His appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), filed on 11 September, went undecided past its 30-day deadline. HELD ALSO No writ against Meta GAC told to decide Restoration has to be sought quickly through a civil suit. No direction to the Union: no clear neglect of a statutory duty was shown. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 02 / 08

WHY NO WRIT UNDER ARTICLE 226 A platform for speech isn't a public duty 1 No public function. A writ lies against private bodies only if they discharge a public duty. Meta doesn't. 2 Influence isn't enough. Instagram shapes public opinion, but public discourse is a consequence of the platform, not a duty it owes. 3 Voluntary and user-driven. Meta isn't legally compelled to offer the service, and no State function has been delegated to it. Meta's operations "remain private in nature." Delhi High Court, Sarthak Bhagat v. Union of India Adv. Ashwani Kumar 03 / 08
